questions.stem: In a classroom extraction of DNA from peas, detergent is added to the crushed peas and later ice-cold ethanol is layered on top. What is the role of the ethanol?
options: Ethanol breaks down the cell membranes and the nuclear envelopes so that the DNA is released
Ethanol digests the proteins that are bound to the DNA in the chromosomes
Ethanol cuts the DNA into short fragments so that it dissolves more easily
DNA is insoluble in cold ethanol, so it comes out of solution and can be collected
questions.explanation: Detergent breaks down membranes to release the DNA, and cold ethanol makes the DNA precipitate as white strands at the boundary, where it can be spooled out. Ethanol does not cut DNA into fragments.

questions.stem: A forensic scientist runs a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on a sample. What is it for?
options: To make many copies of a particular segment of DNA
To separate DNA fragments from each other according to their size
To cut DNA at specific recognition sequences
To join DNA fragments into a bacterial plasmid
questions.explanation: PCR amplifies a chosen DNA segment, producing millions of copies from a very small sample. Separating fragments by size is electrophoresis, cutting is done by restriction enzymes, and joining by ligase.

questions.stem: Why is the reaction mixture in PCR heated to about 95 °C at the start of each cycle?
options: To break the covalent bonds of the sugar-phosphate backbone of each strand
To make the free nucleotides pair up with one another first
To break the hydrogen bonds and separate the two DNA strands
To activate the primers so that they can join to each other
questions.explanation: Heating to about 95 °C breaks the weak hydrogen bonds between bases, so the DNA strands separate and each can act as a template. The strong sugar-phosphate backbone stays intact.

questions.stem: What is the role of primers in PCR?
options: They cut the target sequence out of the original DNA molecule before copying
They prevent the two new strands from pairing with the original strands
They bind to each end of the target sequence and give the polymerase a starting point
They supply all of the energy that the polymerase needs to join the free nucleotides together
questions.explanation: Primers are short single-stranded DNA sequences complementary to the ends of the target region. They bind (anneal) as the mixture cools, and the polymerase extends them by adding free nucleotides.

questions.stem: Why does PCR use a DNA polymerase from bacteria that live in hot springs?
options: It works only at body temperature, so the reaction stops once heated
It can make new DNA without any template, so that no primers are needed in the reaction mixture
It cuts DNA at specific sites, so the target sequence is released
It is heat-resistant, so it is not denatured by the repeated heating to about 95 °C
questions.explanation: The polymerase from heat-loving bacteria such as Thermus aquaticus keeps its shape at high temperatures, so it survives each denaturing step. A typical enzyme would denature and need to be added again every cycle.

questions.stem: A PCR reaction starts with one copy of a target DNA segment. Assuming perfect doubling, how many copies are present after 10 cycles?
questions.explanation: Each cycle doubles the number of copies, so after 10 cycles there are 2 to the power of 10 = 1024 copies. 512 is the number after 9 cycles, and 20 assumes adding two copies per cycle.

questions.stem: Which sequence of temperature steps correctly describes one PCR cycle?
options: About 95 °C to separate strands, about 55 °C for primers to bind, about 72 °C for extension
About 55 °C to separate strands, about 95 °C for primers to bind, about 72 °C for extension
About 72 °C to separate strands, about 95 °C for extension, about 55 °C for primers to bind
About 37 °C to separate strands, about 55 °C for extension, about 95 °C for primers to bind
questions.explanation: Each cycle denatures DNA at about 95 °C, cools to about 50 to 65 °C so primers can anneal, then holds about 72 °C, the optimum for the heat-resistant polymerase to add nucleotides. Primers could not bind at 95 °C, where strands are kept apart.

questions.stem: In gel electrophoresis, why does DNA move towards the positive electrode?
options: Its many bases give it an overall positive charge
Its deoxyribose sugars are attracted by heat
It has no charge and moves with the buffer
Its phosphate groups give it a negative charge
questions.explanation: The phosphate groups in the DNA backbone are negatively charged, so DNA fragments are attracted to the positive electrode. The gel acts as a sieve through which the fragments move.

questions.stem: Fragments of 300, 1200 and 5000 base pairs are separated on the same gel. Which travels furthest from the wells?
options: The 5000 base pair fragment
The 1200 base pair fragment
All travel the same distance
The 300 base pair fragment
questions.explanation: Smaller fragments move more easily through the pores of the gel, so they travel further in a given time. All the fragments have a similar charge per unit length, so size determines how far they move.

questions.stem: Why is a 'ladder' of DNA fragments of known sizes run in one lane of an electrophoresis gel?
options: So the sizes of unknown fragments can be estimated by comparison
So the electric current can flow evenly across the whole gel
So the unknown DNA has enough fragments in it to be made visible
So the gel can be stained without the need for a dye at all
questions.explanation: The ladder acts as a ruler: comparing how far unknown bands travelled with the bands of known size lets the size of each unknown fragment be estimated.

questions.stem: In automated DNA sequencing, each fragment ends in a nucleotide with a coloured label: A green, C blue, G black, T red. Peaks are read from the shortest fragment upwards: green, red, red, blue, black. What is the sequence of the newly made strand?
options: ATTCG
TAAGC
GCTTA
CGAAT
questions.explanation: The electropherogram is read from the shortest fragment to the longest, giving the order of bases added to the new strand: green A, red T, red T, blue C, black G, so ATTCG. The template strand would be complementary to this.

questions.stem: How does the ability to sequence DNA allow scientists to map a species' genome?
options: Sequencing changes genes so that they line up in order on the chromosome
Sequencing counts the number of cells in an organism to find its genes
Sequencing shows the shape of each protein made by the species
Sequences can be pieced together to locate genes along each chromosome
questions.explanation: Genome mapping uses DNA sequencing to determine the order of bases and the positions of genes on each chromosome. Sequencing reads DNA; it does not change it.

questions.stem: In DNA profiling, which regions of DNA are usually compared?
options: Short tandem repeats, whose number of repeats varies between people
Genes for essential enzymes, which are identical in all people in a population
Introns that are identical in every person in a population
Mitochondrial genes that code for the proteins of respiration
questions.explanation: Short tandem repeats (STRs) are non-coding regions where a short sequence is repeated a variable number of times. Comparing the lengths of several STRs gives a profile that is almost unique to each person, except identical twins.

questions.stem: On a DNA profile electropherogram, a person shows only one peak at a particular STR locus. What does this indicate?
options: The PCR reaction failed to copy any DNA from that sample
They inherited the same number of repeats from both parents
They inherited this whole locus from only one of their two parents
The locus is missing from all of the person's chromosomes
questions.explanation: Each person has two alleles at each locus, one from each parent. A single peak means both alleles have the same number of repeats (homozygous); two peaks mean the alleles differ (heterozygous).

questions.stem: At one STR locus, a child has alleles 12 and 15. The mother has alleles 12 and 14. Which man could be the biological father?
options: Man 1: alleles 12 and 14
Man 3: alleles 11 and 14
Man 4: alleles 13 and 16
Man 2: alleles 9 and 15
questions.explanation: The child received one allele from each parent. The mother can only have given 12, so allele 15 must come from the father. Only Man 2 carries 15. In practice many loci are compared before a conclusion is drawn.

questions.stem: A DNA profile from a crime scene matches a suspect at 2 STR loci, while a second suspect matches at all 20 loci tested. Which conclusion is best justified?
options: The second suspect is very likely the source; a 2-locus match is weak evidence
Both suspects are equally likely to be the source of the DNA that was found at the scene
The first suspect must be the source because any match proves identity
Neither suspect can be linked, because profiles cannot be compared at all
questions.explanation: Matching at many independent loci makes it extremely unlikely that an unrelated person would share the profile by chance, so 20 matching loci is strong evidence. Matching at 2 loci is common among unrelated people. A DNA match shows the source of a sample, not guilt.

questions.stem: Which is an ethical issue raised by storing people's DNA profiles in large databases?
options: DNA profiles in databases slowly change, so the stored profiles become wrong after about a year
Databases make PCR unnecessary, so no new samples could ever be tested
Storing profiles alters the DNA of the people whose samples were taken
Privacy and consent, as genetic data could reveal information about relatives
questions.explanation: Genetic information is personal and is shared in part with relatives, raising issues of privacy, consent, possible discrimination by insurers or employers, and who controls the data. Stored profiles do not change, and storage has no effect on a person's DNA.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the action of restriction enzymes?
options: Cut DNA at specific recognition sequences
Join DNA fragments into a single strand
Copy DNA many times over at a high temperature
Add methyl groups to stop transcription
questions.explanation: Restriction enzymes, made by bacteria, recognise particular short base sequences and cut the DNA at or near them. DNA ligase joins fragments, and PCR copies DNA.

questions.stem: The restriction enzyme EcoRI recognises 5' GAATTC 3' and cuts between G and A on each strand. What kind of ends does this produce?
options: Blunt ends with the bases G and C removed completely
Sticky ends with short single-stranded overhangs of AATT
Blunt ends with no single-stranded overhang at all
Sticky ends with single-stranded overhangs of GAATTC on each strand
questions.explanation: Because the cuts on the two strands are staggered, each fragment is left with a single-stranded AATT overhang. These sticky ends can pair with any other fragment cut by the same enzyme.

questions.stem: A gene and a plasmid are both cut with the same restriction enzyme and then mixed. Why is DNA ligase also added?
options: To cut the plasmid open so that the gene can be inserted into it
To form the hydrogen bonds that hold the complementary bases of the sticky ends together
To copy the recombinant plasmid many times before transformation
To join the sugar-phosphate backbones where the sticky ends have paired
questions.explanation: Matching sticky ends pair by hydrogen bonding on their own, but the backbone remains broken. DNA ligase forms covalent bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone, sealing the gene into the plasmid.

questions.stem: How is a DNA probe used to select a particular gene?
options: A labelled single strand binds to the complementary sequence of the gene
A labelled enzyme cuts the gene out of the DNA wherever it finds its base sequence
A labelled primer copies every gene in the sample at the same rate
A labelled plasmid carries the gene into the nucleus of a bacterium
questions.explanation: A probe is a short, labelled (for example fluorescent or radioactive) single-stranded nucleic acid with a sequence complementary to part of the target gene. It binds by base pairing, showing where the gene is so it can be identified and removed.

questions.stem: In genetic engineering, what is a vector?
options: An enzyme that cuts DNA wherever it finds a specific recognition sequence
A gel used to separate DNA fragments according to size
A short primer that starts DNA synthesis in PCR
A carrier, such as a plasmid or virus, that delivers DNA into a cell
questions.explanation: Vectors carry genes into host cells. Plasmids (small circular bacterial DNA) and modified viruses are common vectors. Restriction enzymes cut DNA and primers start PCR.

questions.stem: Bacteria are mixed with recombinant plasmids, then given a brief electric pulse. What does the pulse do?
options: It joins the gene into the plasmid by sealing the sugar-phosphate backbone
It kills the bacteria that do not take up a recombinant plasmid
It makes temporary pores in the membrane so the plasmids can enter
It cuts the plasmids open so they can join the bacterial chromosome
questions.explanation: Electroporation uses a short electric pulse to open temporary pores in cell membranes, allowing DNA to enter. Ligase seals backbones, and selecting transformed cells is usually done with antibiotic resistance genes.

questions.stem: Which technique is usually used to insert a gene into a fertilised animal egg to produce a transgenic animal?
options: Electrophoresis of DNA through an agarose gel
Polymerase chain reaction at high temperature
Transformation of the egg by heat-shocked bacteria
Microinjection of DNA through a fine glass needle
questions.explanation: Microinjection uses a very fine needle to inject DNA directly into the nucleus of a fertilised egg. If the gene is integrated, the animal that develops carries it in all its cells.

questions.stem: Recombinant plasmids carry the gene of interest and an antibiotic resistance gene. After transformation, bacteria are spread on agar containing the antibiotic. What is the purpose?
options: The antibiotic joins the gene of interest into the bacterial chromosome
The antibiotic causes all of the bacteria to take up the plasmids present in the agar
Only bacteria without plasmids survive, so the gene is not expressed
Only bacteria that took up a plasmid survive, so transformed cells are selected
questions.explanation: Transformation is inefficient, so most bacteria take up no plasmid. Bacteria carrying the plasmid also carry the resistance gene, so they survive on antibiotic agar and can be grown on.

questions.stem: Human insulin can be made by genetically modified bacteria. Why does a bacterial cell make the correct human protein from the inserted gene?
options: The genetic code is universal, so bacterial ribosomes read human codons correctly
Bacteria have a nucleus in which they convert each human gene into a bacterial gene
The human gene brings human ribosomes with it into the bacterial cell
Bacteria add introns to the human gene so that it can be translated
questions.explanation: All organisms use the same genetic code, so a human gene's codons specify the same amino acids in a bacterium. For bacterial production, a version of the gene without introns is used, because bacteria cannot remove introns.

questions.stem: Bt cotton, grown in Australia, carries a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. What does this example show?
options: Genes can be transferred between species to produce a transgenic organism
Bacteria can be bred with plants to produce fertile hybrid offspring
Bacterial genes can only ever be expressed in other bacteria and never in any plant
Cotton naturally produces bacterial proteins without any gene transfer
questions.explanation: Bt cotton is transgenic: a gene from another species was inserted so the plant makes a protein toxic to certain insect pests. This reduces the need for some insecticide sprays, although pests may evolve resistance.

questions.stem: Which risk of releasing a transgenic crop requires ongoing monitoring?
options: The crop's genes will turn the soil bacteria into new plant species
The crop cannot reproduce, so its seed will disappear in one season
The inserted gene could spread to related wild plants by cross-pollination
The crop will change the DNA of the people who eat its seeds, oil or other products
questions.explanation: Pollen from a transgenic crop could transfer the new gene to related wild species, with unpredictable effects, so gene flow is monitored. Eating food does not alter a person's DNA.

questions.stem: In CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, what is the role of the Cas9 protein?
options: It cuts both strands of DNA at the target site
It copies the target gene many times over for analysis
It carries the new gene into the nucleus
It joins amino acids into the new protein
questions.explanation: Cas9 is a nuclease that cuts double-stranded DNA. A guide RNA directs it to the target sequence. The cell then repairs the cut, which can disable the gene or insert new DNA.

questions.stem: How does the CRISPR-Cas9 system find the correct place to cut in a genome of billions of base pairs?
options: The target gene is first removed from the cell and placed in a gel
Cas9 cuts randomly until it happens to reach the target sequence
A guide RNA with a complementary sequence pairs with the target DNA
Cas9 recognises the shape of the protein that is made by the target gene
questions.explanation: Scientists design a guide RNA about 20 nucleotides long that is complementary to the target DNA. By base pairing, it directs Cas9 to that specific site.

questions.stem: Scientists cut a faulty gene with CRISPR-Cas9 and add a DNA template carrying the correct sequence. What happens next?
options: The cut remains open permanently, so the gene is never expressed again
The cell's repair system can use the template, inserting the correct sequence
Cas9 translates the template into the correct protein inside the nucleus
The template replaces every copy of the gene in all other organisms of that species
questions.explanation: After Cas9 cuts, the cell repairs the break. If a template with matching ends is present, the repair can copy it, editing in the new sequence. Without a template, repair often introduces small errors that disable the gene.

questions.stem: Where did the CRISPR-Cas system originate in nature?
options: In human white blood cells, as part of the antibody response to infection
In plants, as a way to repair DNA damaged by sunlight
In viruses, as a way to insert their DNA into host cells
In bacteria, as a defence that cuts the DNA of invading viruses
questions.explanation: CRISPR sequences and Cas proteins are part of a bacterial immune system: bacteria store pieces of viral DNA and use them to guide Cas proteins to cut matching viral DNA in later infections. Scientists adapted this into a gene-editing tool.

questions.stem: Which use of CRISPR-Cas9 raises the greatest ethical concern about effects on future generations?
options: Editing the genes of bacteria grown in a sealed laboratory culture
Editing blood stem cells taken from one adult patient with a disease
Editing a gene in cultured cells to study the protein it codes for
Editing the genes of human embryos, so changes pass to descendants
questions.explanation: Editing embryos changes the germline, so the edits are inherited, affecting people who cannot consent and carrying unknown long-term risks. Editing an adult's somatic cells affects only that person.

questions.stem: Scientists use computers to design new proteins that do not exist in nature. Which is a realistic use of such designed proteins?
options: Enzymes that break down pollutants or catalyse industrial reactions
Proteins that turn bacteria into multicellular animals in a single overnight culture
Proteins that change the genetic code of every cell in the body
Enzymes that work at any temperature without ever denaturing
questions.explanation: Because a protein's function depends on its shape, designing amino acid sequences that fold into a chosen shape can produce new enzymes, binding proteins for diagnostics and vaccines, and biomaterials. No protein is immune to denaturation.

questions.stem: A designed protein is intended to bind tightly to one virus protein. Why must its amino acid sequence be chosen so carefully?
options: The sequence determines folding, and the folded shape must match the target
The sequence determines how many copies of the target protein each virus particle carries
Only the first amino acid matters, as it binds to the virus on its own
The sequence decides the colour of the protein when viewed in a gel
questions.explanation: The primary structure determines how a polypeptide folds into its three-dimensional shape, and binding requires a shape complementary to the target. A change in sequence can alter folding and destroy binding.

questions.stem: Why is PCR useful in forensic science?
options: It can make a damaged sample of DNA longer than it was
It can produce enough DNA for analysis from a tiny sample
It can identify a person from fingerprints left at a scene
It can show the exact time a sample was left at the scene
questions.explanation: Forensic samples such as a hair root or a smear of blood may contain very little DNA. PCR amplifies the target regions so that a DNA profile can be made.

questions.stem: Which statement about DNA profiles of identical twins is correct?
options: Their profiles cannot be made, because their DNA cannot be separated
Their profiles are the same, because they developed from one zygote
Their profiles differ at every locus, because they are two people
Their profiles differ, because one inherits all the father's alleles
questions.explanation: Identical twins come from a single fertilised egg, so they share the same DNA sequence and the same STR profile. This is a limitation of standard DNA profiling in forensic cases.
